title: Integer division and remainder
question:
What does this statement print?

std::cout << 7 / 2 << ' ' << 7 % 3;
explanation: Both operands are `int`, so `7 / 2` is integer division, which truncates toward zero and gives 3, and `7 % 3` is the remainder, 1. You only get 3.5 when one operand is floating point (for example `7.0 / 2`), and integer division never rounds up to 4.

title: Narrowing in brace initialization
question: A developer writes `int n{3.7};` to initialize a counter. What does a conforming C++ compiler do?
options: Compiles it and silently truncates the stored value to 3
Compiles it and rounds the stored value to the nearest int, 4
Accepts it with a warning, exactly like `int n = 3.7;`
Diagnoses it: list-initialization forbids this narrowing
explanation: List-initialization (braces) makes narrowing conversions ill-formed, so double to int requires a diagnostic and GCC and Clang reject it as an error. `int n = 3.7;` (copy-initialization) does compile and truncates to 3, which is exactly the silent bug brace-initialization was designed to catch. No implicit conversion here rounds to the nearest value.

title: Comparing signed and unsigned integers
options: not less, because -1 is converted to a huge unsigned value
less, because negative values always compare below positive ones
Nothing; the comparison fails to compile without a cast
It depends on whether the platform uses two's complement
explanation: Under the usual arithmetic conversions, `int` and `unsigned int` have the same rank, so `i` is converted to unsigned and -1 becomes UINT_MAX, which is not less than 1. The code compiles (usually with a -Wsign-compare warning), and the conversion is defined modulo 2^N, so the result does not depend on the platform. C++20's `std::cmp_less(i, u)` performs the mathematically correct comparison.

title: What plain auto deduces from a const reference
question: Given `int x = 1; const int& r = x; auto a = r;`, what is the declared type of `a`?
options: `const int&`, an alias of x
`const int`, a read-only copy
`int`, an independent copy
`int&`, a mutable alias of x
explanation: Plain `auto` follows template argument deduction for a by-value parameter: the reference is stripped and then the top-level const is dropped, so `a` is a modifiable `int` copy. To keep the reference and constness, write `const auto&` or `decltype(auto) a = r;`. `int&` is never deduced here, because a non-const reference cannot bind to a const object.

title: decltype of a parenthesized name
question: With `int x = 0;`, `decltype(x)` is `int`. What is `decltype((x))`, and why?
options: `int`, because extra parentheses never change an expression's type
`int&`, because `(x)` is an lvalue expression, not a plain name
`int&&`, because parentheses turn the name into a temporary value
`const int&`, because parenthesized names are treated as read-only
explanation: For an unparenthesized id-expression, decltype yields the declared type of the entity (`int`). Any other expression follows the value-category rule: an lvalue of type T gives T&, and `(x)` is an lvalue expression, so the result is `int&`. This matters with `decltype(auto)` return types, where `return (x);` accidentally returns a reference to a local.

title: Const pointer versus pointer to const
question: Which declaration allows `*p = 5;` but makes `p = &other;` a compile error?
options: `const int* p = &value;`
`volatile int* p = &value;`
`int* const p = &value;`
`const int* const p = &value;`
explanation: Read declarations right to left: `int* const p` is a const pointer to a mutable int, so the pointee can change but the pointer cannot be reseated. `const int*` (also spelled `int const*`) is a pointer to const int, which forbids `*p = 5` but allows reseating, `const int* const` forbids both, and `volatile` restricts neither.

title: Assigning through a reference
explanation: A reference is bound once, at initialization, and can never be reseated, so `r = b` assigns b's value (2) to a through the alias. Changing b afterwards affects neither a nor r, so both print 2. The answers containing 3 assume `r = b` rebinds r to b, which is how pointer assignment behaves, not references.

title: Pointer arithmetic and negative subscripts
options: It does not compile: negative index
explanation: `arr + 1` points at 20, and pointer arithmetic counts in elements, so `p + 2` points at 40. `p[-1]` is defined as `*(p - 1)`, which is arr[0] = 10; a negative subscript is valid as long as the result stays inside the same array. Answering 30 forgets that p already starts at index 1.

title: Returning a reference to a local
options: It copies the string twice, so it is just slower than returning by value
The returned reference dangles: s is destroyed when the function returns
It fails to compile because a const reference cannot bind to a local
The const qualifier makes the caller unable to read the returned string
explanation: `s` has automatic storage duration and is destroyed when the function returns, so the caller receives a reference to a dead object and any use of it is undefined behavior. The code compiles (compilers usually only warn), and nothing is copied at all. The fix is to return `std::string` by value, which is cheap thanks to copy elision and move semantics.

title: Lifetime extension through a function call
options: Both, because a reference can never extend the life of a temporary
Only A, because B returns a copy that the reference keeps alive
Only B, because extension does not pass through a function's return
Neither, because binding to a const reference always extends lifetime
explanation: Binding a temporary directly to a const reference, as in A, extends the temporary's lifetime to that of the reference. In B, the temporaries are bound to std::max's reference parameters, and std::max returns a reference to one of them, not a new temporary; both are destroyed at the end of the full expression, so r dangles. Capture the result of std::max by value instead.

title: The core idea of RAII
question: What is the core idea of RAII in C++?
options: Bind a resource to an object's lifetime so the destructor releases it
Allocate every object on the heap so a garbage collector can free it later
Release resources by hand at each return path with matching cleanup calls
Reserve all the memory the program needs at startup so allocation never fails
explanation: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) acquires a resource when an object is constructed and releases it in the destructor, so cleanup happens automatically when the object goes out of scope, including during exception unwinding. Standard C++ has no garbage collector, and manual cleanup at every return path is exactly the error-prone pattern RAII replaces. std::unique_ptr, std::lock_guard and std::fstream are typical examples.

title: Releasing new[] memory with delete
question: A buffer is allocated with `int* buf = new int[256];` and later released with `delete buf;`. What is the consequence?
options: Only the first element is freed and the other 255 leak in a well-defined way
Nothing; for built-in types `delete` and `delete[]` are fully interchangeable
The compiler rejects the code because it tracks which form of new was used
Undefined behavior: memory from `new[]` must be released with `delete[]`
explanation: The form of delete must match the form of new: memory from new[] must be released with delete[], otherwise the behavior is undefined, even for trivial types like int. The compiler generally cannot track this, so it compiles, and "only the first element is freed" is a myth, since UB promises nothing. Prefer std::vector<int> or std::unique_ptr<int[]> so the right deallocation happens automatically.

title: When a raw new/delete pair leaks
options: On every call, because `delete` is not allowed to run on a `Widget*`
Whenever process() throws, because the `delete` line is then skipped
Only when the Widget constructor throws partway through construction
Never; the Widget is automatically freed when `w` goes out of scope
explanation: If process() throws, stack unwinding leaves handle() before `delete w;` runs, and a raw pointer has no destructor that frees what it points to. If the Widget constructor itself throws, the new-expression releases the memory automatically, so that case does not leak. The fix is RAII: `auto w = std::make_unique<Widget>();`, or simply a local Widget object.

title: Order of destructor and member destruction
options: ABC
CAB
CBA
BAC
explanation: The body of C's destructor runs first, and then the members are destroyed in reverse order of declaration: b before a. This mirrors construction, where members are initialized in declaration order (a, then b) before the constructor body runs. The reverse order is what lets a later member safely use an earlier one while being destroyed.

title: An exception escaping a destructor
question: A `Logger` destructor calls `flush()`, which can throw. No exception specifications are written anywhere. During a normal scope exit, with no other exception in flight, flush() throws. What happens?
options: std::terminate is called, since destructors are implicitly noexcept
The exception propagates normally to the caller's catch block
The exception is silently swallowed and the object is still destroyed
Behavior is undefined only if a second exception is already active
explanation: Since C++11, a destructor without an explicit specification is implicitly noexcept(true) (unless a base or member destructor may throw), so an exception escaping it calls std::terminate even with no other exception in flight. The "only during unwinding" rule describes pre-C++11 code or a destructor explicitly marked noexcept(false). Handle the error inside the destructor, or expose an explicit close() that can report failures.

title: Copying a std::unique_ptr
options: b shares ownership with a and the reference count becomes 2
b receives a deep copy of the int, so both own separate values
Ownership moves silently to b and a becomes a null pointer
Compilation fails: the unique_ptr copy constructor is deleted
explanation: std::unique_ptr models exclusive ownership, so its copy constructor and copy assignment are deleted and the code does not compile. Transferring ownership must be explicit, `auto b = std::move(a);`, after which a is null. A shared reference count is std::shared_ptr's job, and silent transfer on copy was the flaw of the removed std::auto_ptr.

title: shared_ptr reference count after a scope
explanation: a and b share the same control block, giving a count of 2; c raises it to 3 inside the inner block, and c's destructor brings it back to 2 when the block ends. use_count reports how many shared_ptr instances currently own the object, not how many were ever created.

title: Leaking parent/child shared_ptr trees
question: A `Parent` holds `std::vector<std::shared_ptr<Child>>` and each `Child` holds `std::shared_ptr<Parent> parent`. Memory tools report that every tree leaks after it goes out of scope. What is the idiomatic fix?
options: Call reset() on every child pointer inside the Parent destructor
Replace both pointer types with raw pointers and delete them by hand
Make the back-reference `std::weak_ptr<Parent>` to break the cycle
Switch to std::make_shared so the control block frees the cycle
explanation: Parent and Child own each other, so neither use count can reach zero and neither destructor ever runs, which is also why reset() in Parent's destructor never executes. A std::weak_ptr back-reference observes the parent without owning it (call lock() to use it), so ownership becomes a tree again. make_shared only changes how memory is allocated, not the ownership semantics.

title: What make_shared changes about allocation
question: Compared with `std::shared_ptr<Image>(new Image(...))`, what does `std::make_shared<Image>(...)` typically change about memory?
options: One combined allocation; its memory lingers while weak_ptrs exist
Two separate allocations, but the object memory is freed sooner
The Image is placed on the stack, so no heap allocation happens at all
Nothing; it only saves typing and generates exactly the same allocations
explanation: make_shared typically allocates the object and its control block in a single block, saving an allocation and improving locality. The trade-off: the object's destructor still runs when the last shared_ptr dies, but the combined memory cannot be returned until the last weak_ptr is also gone, which matters for large objects observed by long-lived weak_ptrs. The object still lives on the heap.

title: Creating a shared_ptr from this
question: A `Session` method registers itself with `registry.add(std::shared_ptr<Session>(this));`. Sessions are created with `std::make_shared<Session>()`. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing goes wrong, because both shared_ptrs detect that they share a pointer
Memory leaks since the registry pointer never decrements; call reset() instead
The new pointer is null inside methods; capture a raw `this` pointer instead
Two control blocks mean a double delete; inherit enable_shared_from_this
explanation: Constructing a shared_ptr from a raw pointer creates a new, independent control block, so the object ends up with two reference counts and is deleted twice. Inheriting from std::enable_shared_from_this<Session> and calling shared_from_this() returns a shared_ptr that shares the existing control block. shared_ptrs never detect each other by address.

title: Calling a non-virtual function via a base pointer
options: Base
Derived
BaseDerived
Nothing; the call is ambiguous
explanation: f is not virtual, so the call is bound at compile time using the static type of p, which is Base*; Derived::f merely hides Base::f. Only declaring Base::f virtual makes the call dispatch on the dynamic type and print "Derived". There is no ambiguity, because lookup through Base* finds exactly one f.

title: Deleting through a base without a virtual destructor
question: `Base` has a public non-virtual destructor, and `Derived` owns a `std::vector<char>` buffer. Code does `Base* b = new Derived; delete b;`. What is the problem?
options: Only Base's members leak, since the vector frees Derived's own storage
Undefined behavior; in practice Derived's destructor is usually skipped
It fails to compile because Base* cannot be deleted without a cast
Nothing, because delete always runs the destructor of the most-derived class
explanation: Deleting a derived object through a pointer to a base whose destructor is not virtual is undefined behavior; typically only ~Base runs, so Derived's members, such as the vector's buffer, are never released. Make the base destructor public and virtual, or protected and non-virtual if deletion through Base* should be impossible (Core Guidelines C.35). The code compiles cleanly, which is why this bug survives reviews.

title: Passing a derived object by value
options: Derived, because virtual calls always use the original object's type
Nothing; passing a Derived where a Base is expected does not compile
Base, because the parameter is a sliced copy holding only the Base part
Either one, because the result depends on the compiler's vtable layout
explanation: Passing by value copy-constructs a brand-new Base from the Base subobject of d, slicing off the Derived part; inside show the object's dynamic type really is Base, so Base::name runs. The derived-to-base conversion is implicit, so it compiles, and the behavior is fully defined. Take `const Base&` (or a pointer) to keep polymorphic behavior (Core Guidelines ES.63).

title: Virtual call inside a base constructor
options: Derived Derived
Base Base
Derived Base
Base Derived
explanation: While Base's constructor runs, the Derived part does not exist yet, so the object's dynamic type is Base and the virtual call resolves to Base::hello. After construction completes, d.hello() dispatches to Derived::hello. This is why Core Guidelines C.82 says not to call virtual functions in constructors and destructors: the override you expect is not the one called.

title: A logging destructor that turned moves into copies
question: To debug a leak, someone adds `~Buffer() { log("freed"); }` to a class whose only member is a `std::vector<int>` and which previously declared no special members. Afterwards, profiling shows `Buffer b2 = std::move(b1);` doing a full vector copy. Why?
options: A declared destructor suppresses the implicit move constructor
std::move is ignored for classes with a user-provided destructor
Logging in a destructor makes the compiler disable copy elision
The vector's move constructor stops being noexcept in this case
explanation: When a class user-declares a destructor, the compiler no longer implicitly declares a move constructor or move assignment, but it still generates the copy constructor, so the rvalue from std::move binds to it and copies the vector. Following the rule of zero, or the rule of five by adding `Buffer(Buffer&&) = default;` and its siblings, restores moves. Copy elision is unrelated because b1 is an existing named object.

title: Deducing one T from two different arguments
question: Given `template<typename T> T maxOf(T a, T b);`, what happens with the call `maxOf(1, 2.5)`?
options: T is deduced as double and the int argument is converted implicitly
It fails to compile, because T deduces to int and to double
T is deduced as int and 2.5 is truncated to 2 with a narrowing warning
T is deduced as the common type of both arguments, std::common_type
explanation: Each argument deduces T independently, int from 1 and double from 2.5, and conflicting deductions make deduction fail, so there is no viable function and the call does not compile. Implicit conversions are not considered while deducing T. Fix it with `maxOf<double>(1, 2.5)`, by converting an argument, or with two template parameters and std::common_type.

title: Template defined in a .cpp file fails to link
question: A team declares `template<class T> T clamp01(T v);` in `math.h`, defines it in `math.cpp`, and calls `clamp01(0.5)` from `main.cpp`. Everything compiles, but linking fails with an undefined reference. Why?
options: Templates cannot be declared in a header and must live in exactly one .cpp file
The linker needs the `export` keyword on every template to find its symbols
math.cpp never instantiates clamp01<double>, and main.cpp cannot see the body
Function templates have internal linkage, so calls across files always fail
explanation: A template is instantiated where it is used, which requires the definition to be visible there. main.cpp only sees the declaration, so it emits a call to clamp01<double> expecting another file to provide it, while math.cpp never uses clamp01<double> and therefore never instantiates it. Put the definition in the header, or add the explicit instantiation `template double clamp01(double);` to math.cpp.

title: Why if constexpr skips the invalid branch
options: The discarded branch of `if constexpr` is not instantiated for that T
The optimizer removes the dead branch before type checking takes place
Templates are never type-checked unless the function is actually called
Calls to missing member functions are resolved lazily at run time
explanation: With `if constexpr`, the condition is a constant expression and, inside a template, the discarded statement is not instantiated, so `v.size()` is never checked for T = int. With a plain `if`, both branches are instantiated and the call fails to compile even though the condition is known. Optimization happens after semantic checking, and C++ has no run-time member lookup.

title: Using a nested type of a template parameter
options: Add `template` before `C::value_type`, because it names a nested template
Write `typename C::value_type`; dependent names default to non-types
Replace `const C&` with `C&`, because front() cannot be called on const
Add `using namespace std;` so the compiler can find the value_type alias
explanation: Inside a template, a qualified name that depends on a template parameter is assumed not to name a type unless it is prefixed with `typename`, so the line cannot be parsed as a declaration. C++20 dropped that requirement in some contexts where only a type can appear, such as alias declarations, but a local variable declaration still needs it. The `template` keyword is for dependent member templates, and std::vector::front has a const overload.

title: Function template specialization versus overloading
options: It fails to compile: the call is ambiguous
explanation: The explicit specialization `f(int*)` specializes the first template, f(T), because it is the only primary template declared at that point. Overload resolution considers only primary templates: f(T*) is more specialized than f(T) for an int*, so it wins and prints 3, and the specialization of f(T) is never used. This is why overloading function templates is usually preferred to specializing them.

title: Container for constant-time key lookup
question: You need to look up user sessions by string ID millions of times, and iteration order does not matter. Which standard container gives average O(1) lookup?
options: std::map
std::vector with std::find
std::set
std::unordered_map
explanation: std::unordered_map is a hash table with average constant-time find, insert and erase (linear in the worst case with a bad hash). std::map and std::set are ordered, typically red-black trees, with O(log n) operations, and std::find on a vector is a linear scan. Choose std::map only when you need sorted iteration or range queries by key.

title: Reading a missing key with map::operator[]
options: It throws std::out_of_range
Undefined behavior: the key is missing
explanation: map::operator[] inserts a value-initialized element (0 for int) when the key is absent and returns a reference to it, so it prints 0 and the size becomes 1. That is also why it cannot be used on a const map. Use find() or contains() (C++20) to test for a key without inserting, or at(), which throws std::out_of_range.

title: Vector size after std::remove
explanation: std::remove only shifts the kept elements to the front and returns an iterator to the new logical end; algorithms work on iterators and cannot change a container's size. The size stays 5 and the tail holds valid but unspecified values. Use the erase-remove idiom `v.erase(std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 0), v.end())` or, since C++20, `std::erase(v, 0)`.

title: Growing a vector while iterating it
options: push_back appends past end(), so the loop can never terminate
Using != instead of < lets `it` skip over end()
push_back can reallocate the storage, invalidating `it`
Dereferencing `it` after `++it` reads an element out of order
explanation: When the size exceeds the capacity, push_back reallocates and moves the elements to new storage, invalidating all iterators, references and pointers into the vector; continuing to use `it` is undefined behavior, which explains the intermittent crash. Comparing with `<` instead of `!=` would not help. Iterate by index, or collect the new values in a separate vector and append them after the loop.

title: A std::sort comparator that crashes
options: std::sort needs a comparator returning int, like C's qsort does
Lambdas with reference parameters cannot be passed to std::sort
std::sort is not stable, so equal elements cause it to loop forever
`<=` is not a strict weak ordering, so the behavior is undefined
explanation: The comparator must be a strict weak ordering: comp(a, a) must be false, and `<=` returns true for equal elements. Implementations rely on that guarantee to skip bounds checks in inner loops, so violating it is undefined behavior that can read past the range and crash. Use `<`; stability is a separate property (std::stable_sort) and is not a source of crashes.

title: What std::move does on its own
question: What does `std::move(x)` do by itself?
options: It casts x to an rvalue so that move overloads can be selected
It transfers x's resources into a new temporary object right away
It marks x as destroyed so its destructor will not run later
It swaps x with a default-constructed object of the same type
explanation: std::move is just a cast to an rvalue reference (it produces an xvalue) and moves nothing. The transfer only happens if the result initializes or is assigned to an object whose move constructor or move assignment then takes the resources. x is still destroyed normally at the end of its scope.

title: What is guaranteed about a moved-from string
question: After `std::string t = std::move(s);`, which statement about `s` does the standard library guarantee?
options: s is guaranteed to be empty, so s.size() always returns 0
Any use of s, including s.clear(), is undefined behavior
s keeps its previous contents because the move only copied it
s is valid but unspecified; you can assign to it or clear it
explanation: Standard library objects are left in a valid but unspecified state after being moved from: their invariants hold, so operations without preconditions such as assignment, clear() or size() are fine, but you cannot rely on the value. Most implementations leave the string empty in practice, but that is not guaranteed. Reassign the object before relying on its contents.

title: std::move on a const object
question: A 1 MB buffer is declared `const std::string payload = load();` and later passed as `queue.push(std::move(payload));`. Profiling shows a full copy. Why?
options: std::move is a no-op unless optimizations such as -O2 are enabled
It yields `const std::string&&`, which binds to the copy constructor
push() always copies its argument, regardless of the value category
Strings under a few MB are always copied by the small-string optimization
explanation: Casting a const object yields a const rvalue; the move constructor takes a non-const `std::string&&` and cannot bind to it, so overload resolution picks the copy constructor taking `const std::string&`. Do not declare an object const if you intend to move from it later. The small-string optimization only applies to short strings, and std::move behaves the same at every optimization level.

title: Vector reallocation with a throwing move constructor
question: A `std::vector<Order>` grows past its capacity. `Order` has a user-defined copy constructor and a move constructor that is not marked noexcept. How are the existing elements transferred to the new buffer?
options: They are moved, because moving is always cheaper than copying
They are moved one by one, and copied only if a move throws
They are copied, preserving the strong exception guarantee
Neither; vector reallocation relocates the raw bytes
explanation: To keep push_back's strong exception guarantee, vector relocates elements with std::move_if_noexcept: if the move constructor may throw and a copy constructor exists, it copies, because a move that throws halfway would leave the old buffer damaged. Marking the move constructor noexcept (Core Guidelines C.66) lets reallocation move instead. std::vector does not relocate raw bytes for types that are not trivially copyable.

title: std::move on a forwarding reference
options: push_back takes its argument by value, so name is always consumed
T&& in a template is an rvalue reference and only binds to rvalues
store must be declared before add, so a temporary copy was moved
v is a forwarding reference; use std::forward<T>(v), not std::move
explanation: In `template<class T> void add(T&& v)`, T&& is a forwarding reference: passing the lvalue `name` deduces T = std::string&, so v refers to the caller's string, and std::move(v) unconditionally moves from it. `std::forward<T>(v)` moves only when the caller passed an rvalue and copies otherwise. A non-template `std::string&&` parameter, by contrast, would not accept `name` at all.

title: Destroying a joinable std::thread
options: The thread is detached automatically and keeps running on its own
std::terminate is called because t is still joinable
The destructor of t blocks until work() has finished, then returns
work() is cancelled immediately and its stack is unwound safely
explanation: Destroying a std::thread that is still joinable (neither joined nor detached) calls std::terminate. Joining on destruction is the behavior of C++20's std::jthread, which also requests a stop first, and std::thread never detaches or cancels on its own. Call t.join() before t goes out of scope, or use std::jthread.

title: Lost updates on a shared counter
question: Two threads each run `for (int i = 0; i < 100000; ++i) ++counter;` on a shared `int counter`. The final value is often below 200000. What is the correct diagnosis and fix?
options: The int overflows; changing counter to long long fixes the result
Marking counter `volatile` makes each increment atomic across threads
It is a data race (undefined behavior); use std::atomic<int> or a mutex
The threads need a std::this_thread::yield() call after each increment
explanation: `++counter` is a read-modify-write, and unsynchronized conflicting accesses from two threads are a data race, which is undefined behavior; lost updates are the typical symptom. std::atomic<int>, whose ++ is an atomic fetch_add, or a std::mutex fixes it. volatile provides no atomicity or inter-thread ordering in C++, and 200000 fits easily in an int.

title: Deadlock when locking two mutexes
question: `transfer(a, b)` locks `a.m` and then `b.m` with two lock_guards, and occasionally deadlocks while another thread runs `transfer(b, a)`. What is the simplest standard fix?
options: Lock both at once with `std::scoped_lock lock(a.m, b.m);`
Replace both lock_guards with `std::unique_lock` objects
Make both mutexes `std::recursive_mutex` so they can relock
Add a `std::this_thread::sleep_for` between the two locks
explanation: The two threads acquire the same pair of mutexes in opposite orders, the classic lock-ordering deadlock. std::scoped_lock (C++17) acquires several mutexes with a deadlock-avoidance algorithm, like std::lock, so the order of the arguments no longer matters. unique_lock alone does not change the ordering, recursive_mutex only helps when the same thread relocks one mutex, and sleeping merely changes the timing.

title: Consumer wakes up to an empty queue
question: A consumer runs `std::unique_lock lk(m); cv.wait(lk); auto job = q.front();` and occasionally reads from an empty queue. What is the fix?
options: Call notify_all instead of notify_one in the producer thread
Use a std::lock_guard instead, because wait needs a non-movable lock
Release the lock before calling wait so producers can enqueue
Wait with a predicate: `cv.wait(lk, [&]{ return !q.empty(); });`
explanation: wait can return because of a spurious wakeup, or after another consumer has already taken the item, so the condition must be rechecked under the lock; the predicate overload runs `while (!pred()) wait(lk);` for you. notify_all wakes more waiters and makes the race worse, wait requires a std::unique_lock because it must unlock the mutex, and it releases the mutex itself while blocked (Core Guidelines CP.42).

title: Publishing data with a relaxed atomic flag
question: Thread A writes `data = 42;` then `ready.store(true, std::memory_order_relaxed);`. Thread B spins on `ready.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)` and then reads `data`, a plain int. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; atomics are sequentially consistent regardless of the order passed
Relaxed gives no happens-before, so reading data races; use release/acquire
The store must be seq_cst; acquire and release orders only apply to mutexes
B must use compare_exchange_strong instead of load to observe the flag
explanation: Relaxed operations are atomic but impose no ordering, so seeing ready == true does not make the earlier write to data visible, and the non-atomic accesses to data form a data race (undefined behavior). A release store paired with an acquire load that reads the stored value creates a happens-before edge that publishes data. seq_cst is only the default when no order is passed, and acquire and release are memory orders for atomic operations.

title: Configuring and building out of source
question: Which pair of commands configures a CMake project into a separate `build` directory and then builds it?
options: `cmake --configure build` followed by `cmake --make build`
`cmake --init .` followed by `cmake --run build`
`cmake -S . -B build` followed by `cmake --build build`
`cmake --build .` followed by `cmake -B build`
explanation: `-S` names the source directory and `-B` the build directory, which keeps generated files out of the source tree, and `cmake --build <dir>` then drives the underlying build tool (Make, Ninja, MSBuild) portably. The order matters: a build tree must be configured before `--build` can run, and `--configure`, `--make`, `--init` and `--run` are not CMake options.

title: Requiring C++20 for a CMake target
question: In a CMakeLists.txt, which line reliably requires C++20 for the `app` target on any supported compiler?
options: `target_compile_features(app PUBLIC cxx_std_20)`
`add_definitions(-DCXX_STANDARD=20)`
`set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS "-std=c++20")`
`project(app VERSION 20)`
explanation: target_compile_features with the cxx_std_20 meta-feature tells CMake that the target needs at least C++20, and CMake adds the right flag for whichever compiler is used (setting the CXX_STANDARD property with CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON also works). Hard-coding -std=c++20 breaks MSVC, which uses /std:c++20, add_definitions only defines a preprocessor macro, and project VERSION is the project's own version number.

title: Keeping a dependency out of consumers' builds
question: The `net` library uses OpenSSL only inside its .cpp files; its public headers never include OpenSSL. How should `net` link it so that targets using `net` do not inherit OpenSSL's include paths?
options: `target_link_libraries(net PUBLIC OpenSSL::SSL)`
`target_link_libraries(net INTERFACE OpenSSL::SSL)`
`link_libraries(OpenSSL::SSL)` at the top level
`target_link_libraries(net PRIVATE OpenSSL::SSL)`
explanation: A PRIVATE dependency is used to build net itself, but its usage requirements, such as include directories and compile definitions, are not propagated to targets that link to net. PUBLIC would propagate them too, which is right only when net's headers expose OpenSSL types, and INTERFACE propagates to consumers without using the library for net itself. link_libraries affects every target created after it.

title: Function defined in a header breaks linking
question: `util.h` contains `int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }` and is included by `a.cpp` and `b.cpp`. Both compile, but linking fails. What fixes it while keeping the body in the header?
options: Wrap the header in `#pragma once` so it is only included once
Mark the function `inline` so identical definitions may repeat
Declare the function `extern` so the linker merges the symbols
Move `#include "util.h"` below all other includes in both files
explanation: Each .cpp file is a separate translation unit, so each one emits its own external definition of add, violating the One Definition Rule, and the linker reports a multiple definition. `inline` allows one identical definition per translation unit. Include guards and #pragma once only prevent double inclusion within a single translation unit, and `extern` is already the default linkage for functions.

title: CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE ignored by a multi-config generator
question: A CI job runs `cmake -S . -B build -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` and then `cmake --build build`, yet the binaries land in `build/Debug`. Why?
options: CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE must be set inside CMakeLists.txt, not on the command line
Release builds require `-DCMAKE_CONFIGURATION_TYPES=Release` on every run
Visual Studio is multi-config; pick the config with `--config Release`
The variable is ignored when the build directory name is not `Release`
explanation: Multi-config generators (Visual Studio, Xcode, Ninja Multi-Config) generate every configuration at once and ignore CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE; the configuration is chosen at build time with `cmake --build build --config Release`, and Debug is used when none is given. Single-config generators such as Makefiles and Ninja are the ones that honor CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE at configure time, and it can be set on the command line.

title: Which integer overflow is well-defined
question: Which of these expressions has well-defined behavior in standard C++ (with a 32-bit int)?
options: `UINT_MAX + 1u`, which wraps around to 0
`INT_MAX + 1`, which wraps around to INT_MIN
`-INT_MIN`, which evaluates to INT_MAX + 1
`1 << 40`, which keeps only the low 32 bits
explanation: Unsigned arithmetic is defined modulo 2^N, so `UINT_MAX + 1u` is exactly 0. Signed overflow, as in `INT_MAX + 1` or `-INT_MIN` (whose result is not representable), is undefined behavior even though C++20 mandates two's complement representation, and shifting by at least the bit width of the promoted operand is undefined as well.

title: Out-of-range access with [] versus at()
question: Given `std::vector<int> v(5);`, what is the difference between `v[10]` and `v.at(10)`?
options: Both throw std::out_of_range, but `v[10]` also logs a debug message
`v[10]` returns 0 for missing elements, while `v.at(10)` throws
Both grow the vector to 11 elements and return a value-initialized int
`v[10]` is undefined behavior, while `v.at(10)` throws out_of_range
explanation: operator[] performs no bounds checking, so an out-of-range index is undefined behavior: it may read garbage, crash, or appear to work. at() checks the index and throws std::out_of_range. Unlike std::map::operator[], vector's operator[] never inserts elements. Debug or hardened standard library modes can add checks to [], but you should not rely on that.

title: Writing through a cast string literal
question: Legacy code does `char* p = (char*)"hello"; p[0] = 'H';`. It compiles but crashes on some platforms. Why?
options: The cast copies the literal to the heap, and that copy is never freed
String literals are const arrays; writing to one is undefined behavior
p[0] is out of bounds because literals start at index 1 in C++
The 'H' character literal has type int, so the write is truncated
explanation: A string literal has type const char[N] and may live in read-only memory (identical literals may even be shared), so modifying it is undefined behavior; the C-style cast only hides the const. If you need a mutable buffer, use `char s[] = "hello";` or std::string. In C++ a character literal such as 'H' has type char, not int as in C.

title: An overflow check removed by the optimizer
question: The check `if (len + 100 < len) return error;`, where `len` is an `int`, disappears from the -O2 binary. What explains it?
options: A compiler bug: optimizers must never delete explicit checks
The check was folded because len is always positive at -O2
Signed overflow is UB, so the compiler may assume it is always false
Comparisons on int are evaluated in 64-bit registers, so it never overflows
explanation: Because signed overflow is undefined, the optimizer may assume `len + 100` never overflows, which makes `len + 100 < len` provably false and the branch dead. Write the check so it cannot overflow, for example `if (len > INT_MAX - 100)`, or use unsigned arithmetic, where wraparound is defined. Compilers are allowed to assume UB never happens, so this is not a bug.

title: Reading a float's bits without breaking aliasing
question: To read a float's bit pattern, code does `std::uint32_t bits = *reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t*>(&f);`. At -O2 it returns stale values at some inlined call sites. What is the standard-conforming fix?
options: Mark f as volatile so the compiler always reloads it from memory
Use a union and read the inactive member, which C++ fully supports
Use static_cast<std::uint32_t>(f), which preserves the exact bits
Use std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f) (C++20) or std::memcpy
explanation: Accessing a float object through a uint32_t glvalue violates the type-aliasing rules, so it is undefined behavior and the optimizer may assume the two never alias. std::bit_cast (C++20), or memcpy into a uint32_t, copies the object representation legally and compiles to the same instruction. Reading an inactive union member is UB in C++ (unlike C), and static_cast converts the value (3.7f becomes 3), not the bits.

title: Structured bindings over a std::map
question: What does `for (const auto& [name, score] : scores)` do when `scores` is a `std::map<std::string, int>`?
options: Copies each key into name and sorts the scores into a new vector
Binds name and score to each pair's key and value, no copies
Declares a two-element array called name with score as its size
Creates a lambda capture list for name and score in every pass
explanation: Structured bindings (C++17) introduce names that refer to the members of the object being decomposed. With `const auto&`, the hidden variable is a reference to each std::pair<const std::string, int>, so name and score alias its first and second members without copying. The square brackets have nothing to do with arrays or lambda captures here.

title: Reading a std::optional with a default
question: `std::optional<int> findPort(const Config&);` may find no port. How do you read the result with a default of 8080?
options: `findPort(cfg).get_or_default(8080)`
`findPort(cfg) ?: 8080`
`findPort(cfg).value_or(8080)`
`findPort(cfg).value(8080)`
explanation: value_or returns the contained value if there is one and the given fallback otherwise. `?:` with an omitted middle operand is a GNU extension, not standard C++, and std::optional has no get_or_default member. value() takes no arguments: it returns the value or throws std::bad_optional_access when the optional is empty.

title: A string_view over a temporary string
options: The concatenated temporary dies at the end of the statement
string_view cannot be constructed from std::string, only from literals
string_view copies the characters, so the log shows a stale snapshot
The + operator returns a string_view that has no null terminator
explanation: std::string_view is a non-owning view; here it points into the temporary std::string produced by operator+, which is destroyed at the end of the full expression, so log(sv) reads freed memory. string_view does convert from std::string, never copies the characters, and operator+ returns a std::string. Keep the std::string in a named variable, and use string_view mainly for function parameters.

title: Calling a constrained template with the wrong type
question: Given `template<std::integral T> T half(T x) { return x / 2; }`, what happens with `half(2.5)`?
options: It returns 1.25 because the concept is only a documentation hint
It fails to compile: double does not satisfy std::integral
It compiles and converts 2.5 to int, so the call returns 1
It throws std::invalid_argument at run time for the double
explanation: A constrained template parameter is checked during overload resolution: double does not satisfy std::integral, so the template is not viable and the call fails with an error naming the unsatisfied constraint. Concepts are enforced rather than documentation, they never insert conversions to make a template viable, and they have no run-time behavior.

title: Calling a consteval function with a run-time value
options: It compiles and square runs at run time, like a constexpr function
It compiles, but square(k) returns 0 because k is unknown at compile time
It compiles only with optimizations on, which fold the call to a constant
It fails: a consteval call must produce a compile-time constant
explanation: consteval declares an immediate function: every call must be a constant expression evaluated at compile time, and `square(k)` depends on a value read at run time, so the program is ill-formed. A constexpr function would silently fall back to run-time evaluation here, which is exactly the difference between the two. Optimization levels never change whether a program is well-formed.

title: Pointer into a growing vector
options: push_back may reallocate the buffer, leaving first dangling
Taking the address of a vector element is undefined behavior
std::cout cannot print a value that is read through a raw pointer
push_back shifts existing elements one slot to the right
explanation: When push_back exceeds the current capacity, the vector allocates a new buffer, moves the elements and frees the old one, invalidating all pointers, references and iterators to elements. Reading through first is then a use-after-free. Taking element addresses is fine while no reallocation happens; call reserve() up front or keep indices instead of pointers.
